screenings.title: zi
screenings.description: “Poetic, political, and above all incontrovertibly material” [The New Yorker], Kogonada’s fourth feature, the experimental drama zi, follows the title character, played by Michelle Mao, a concert violinist whose aimless peregrinations through the streets of Hong Kong are interrupted by visions of what may be either her past or future, a condition she attempts to explain to a new American acquaintance (Haley Lu Richardson, Columbus) while a stranger (Jin Ha) observes the pair from a distance. A valentine to the textures and colors of the Fragrant Harbor as seen by night, featuring music by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto, the formally audacious, shot-on-the-fly zi is a film of unusual delicacy and reserve, one whose air of mystery abides long after the credits have rolled.

screenings.description: Based on the true story of boxer Ogasawara Keiko, Miyake’s unorthodox-stance sports film stars a superb Kishii Yukino as the deaf-from-birth Keiko, seeing the possibility of her still-young professional career in grave peril, along with the boxing gym that’s her second home, when the pandemic threatens to erode her self-worth and shutter the place that’s done so much to provide her with a sense of resolve. “A highly atypical boxing drama that is less concerned with the glory of the knockout punch, and more with the interior decisions and indecisions that occur long before the punch is thrown, and long after the punch has landed… Tough and tender.” —Sight & Sound

screenings.title: Midnight Cowboy
screenings.description: Dir. John Schlesinger. 1969, 113 mins. U.S. 4K DCP. With Dustin Hoffman, Jon Voight, Sylvia Miles, Brenda Vaccaro. John Voight’s wannabe gigolo Joe Buck leaves Texas and winds up hustling on 42nd Street, bonding with the blighted block’s genius loci, Dustin Hoffman’s tubercular petty thief Ratzo Rizzo. Adapting a book by James Leo Herlihy, screenwriter Waldo Salt and British director John Schlesinger (in his first American film) fashioned something so brutally honest and daring that it became an instant sensation. Probably the most desperately romantic New York movie of its era, John Schlesinger’s astonishing, downtrodden Midnight Cowboy won three Oscars including Best Picture despite being the first major studio production released with an X. screenings.title: White Snail
screenings.description: NEW YORK PREMIERE! FILMMAKERS IN PERSON!“Following two unconventional documentaries – SPACE DOGS (2019) and DREAMING DOGS (2024) – focused on the lives of stray canines, filmmaking duo Elsa Kremser and Levin Peter return with the narrative feature WHITE SNAIL, where the two protagonists also exhibit a fondness for various animals. Set in contemporary Belarus, the film tells the story of Masha, a blonde, thin, fair-skinned model pursuing her dream job in China, and Misha, a tattooed, thickset painter working at a morgue. Played with extreme naturalness by non-professionals Marya Imbro and Mikhail Senkov, these two loners strike up an unlikely but profound friendship that will force them to confront their secrets and wounds. The worlds to which Masha and Misha belong are completely at odds. But as these characters form a strange bond, the fashion industry and the funeral business reveal equally unlikely coincidences and areas of overlap that subtly proliferate as the plot advances. By depicting how we and our bodies relate to sight and touch, life and death, reality and imagination, flaws and perfection, Kremser and Peter map two universes on to one another, leaving the viewer to determine where they intersect and whether they diverge.” –Cristina Álvarez López, VIENNALEThese screenings are co-presented by Deutsches Haus at NYU and Erste Bank, on the occasion of the co-awarding of the 2025 Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to WHITE SNAIL. Since 2011, each annual edition of the Viennale (Vienna International FilmFestival) has featured the granting of the Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to one or more filmmakers whose films are included within the festival. Designed to showcase the best of Austrian cinema, the Award was founded by Erste Bank, the Viennale’s main sponsor, and is awarded according to the findings of an independent jury. The Award brings a cash prize as well as a residency as a visiting filmmaker organized by Deutsches Haus at NYU. Additional support for these screenings has been provided by the Austrian Cultural Forum New York.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Asako I & II
screenings.description: Following up Happy Hour, his justly acclaimed epic of everyday life, Hamaguchi offers a different but no less quietly revolutionary vision with this pop romance that moves from youthful exuberance and delusion to mature circumspection and compromise, while keeping up throughout a magical tonal balance of wistfulness, comic buoyancy, and the ineffably heartbreaking. As a student in Osaka, Asako meets and falls in love with a drifter named Baku who one day drifts right out of her life. Two years later, working in Tokyo, she sees Baku again—or, rather, a young, solid businessman named Ryohei who is Baku’s double in every respect save personality. After initial astonishment, they begin to build a life together—but a twist in circumstances threatens to tear it all down, and forces Asako to confront her long, lingering love affair with a half-ghost fantasy.

screenings.description: Alone for the holiday while his wife and children are on vacation, the staid, middle-aged college professor Richard Wanley (Edward G. Robinson) is about to settle in to an uneventful stretch of nights spent sipping port by the fireplace of his club—but then he catches a glimpse of a beguiling brunette in a gallery window and, in short order, finds himself having a drink with the model (Joan Bennett), after which everything goes straight to hell. Involved in a self-defense killing and its subsequent cover-up, Wanley finds himself investigating his own crime at the elbow of fellow clubman and D.A. Frank Lalor (Raymond Massey), the noose tightening around his neck with the emergence of every fresh clue and misstep. A high-style turning-of-the-screws noir suspenser, with a wonderfully oleaginous turn from heel extraordinaire Dan Duryea.

screenings.description: Argento’s return to his giallo roots after veering off into gonzo horror/fantasy, Tenebrae features Anthony Franciosa as an American author of potboiler thrillers who, promoting a new book in Rome, finds that a murderer is re-enacting his most ghoulish delights of literary fancy. Argento uses the occasion to scale new, dizzying heights of his own, employing bravura crane shots, brazenly baroque lighting, and the iconic moment of a razor slashing through white cotton.

screenings.title: The Brood
screenings.description: In The Brood, the bitter divorce between the mentally disturbed Nola (Samantha Eggar) and her ex-husband Frank (Art Hindle) was pretty messy, so it should be a good sign that she’s finally getting professional help from the renowned Dr. Hal Raglan (Oliver Reed)—but Frank can’t help but notice that people on Nola’s long list of enemies keep dying at the hands of asexual, dwarfish assassins, and so he starts to wonder what exactly the experimental therapy practiced at Dr. Raglan’s Somafree Institute consists of… Written while Cronenberg was in the midst of his own divorce and custody battle, The Brood is a brutal, bracing airing of anxieties gussied up in grindhouse trappings.

screenings.title: Filipiñana
screenings.description: Amid stifling heat and pervasive drought, Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto), a 17-year-old Ilokana from the rural north, works at a posh country club outside Manila, lining up golf balls for powerful men to drive into the verdant horizon. New to the job, she wanders the immaculate grounds sampling its luxuries as members, including an industrialist and his expatriate niece, the club president and his pampered wife, and a slew of Chinese tourists, engage in a complex dance with the club’s doting and subservient staff. But something is rotting beneath the pristine fairways of the elite resort, as Isabel discovers when she tries to return a mislaid golf club to its patriarchal director, Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman). The deeper she journeys into its most exclusive corners, the closer she gets to the violent truths of the club, her native Philippines, and her own past.

screenings.title: Spellbound
screenings.description: Hitchcock goes in for psychoanalysis in this singular thriller, made under the influence of Sigmund Freud and Salvador Dalí, the latter of whom designed the dazzling dream sequence. Analyst Ingrid Bergman falls for amnesiac patient Gregory Peck—but is there a murderer’s heart lurking beneath that dapper exterior? The delirium only grows more intense and Miklós Rózsa’s theremin-inflected score becomes more urgent as her doubts grow and she draws closer to the truth.

screenings.title: The General
screenings.description: Keaton’s engineer Johnnie Gray is another of his big-hearted little guys, rejected by the Confederate Army, though when the Union tries to make off with his train, runt Johnnie shows his mettle in the most incredible sustained chase sequence in all of silent comedy. Wall-to-wall with elaborate, antic gags, though also marked by a quiet sense of pastoral beauty that had previously been given little outlet.

screenings.title: The Killing
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1956. 85 mins. 35mm. With Sterling Hayden, Coleen Gray, Vince Edwards, Jay C. Flippen, Elisha Cook Jr., Marie Windsor. Stanley Kubrick and pulp-fiction legend Jim Thompson co-wrote this darkly comic thriller about a racetrack heist gone awry. With its thick layers of irony and stopwatch-precise playing with time, Kubrick’s fragmented crime noir (whose existential overtones and intricate structure inspired Quentin Tarantino’s Reservoir Dogs) is his true narrative breakthrough, laying the groundwork for a filmography of flawed, failed masculinity and fatalistic humor. screenings.title: Small File Media Festival: Screening and Workshop
screenings.description: Part of MoMI Lab Bringing together an international community of artists pioneering small-file eco-media, the Small File Media Festival (SFMF) comes to New York City for the first time for this free screening and workshop. “An all-out intervention to save the world, one pixel at a time,” SFMF raises awareness around the high carbon footprint of streaming media with its annual showcase of small-file treasures. Small-file videos run at 1.44 MB per minute by harnessing a range of techniques, from filming with obsolete cameras to compressing video with open-source algorithms. Designed for lightness and resilience, this tiny bitrate allows the small file to thrive in places where electricity and internet access are precarious. The selected shorts in this program showcase the breadth and depth of the small-file video for those who never considered the future could be so small. It includes contemplative home videos, experimental animations, poetic revelations, and pixelated dreams. The screening will be followed by a workshop inviting participants to make their own small-file videos with an introduction to various video compression techniques. This program invites participants to collectively, radically, and creatively rethink computational culture and sustainability practices. Schedule 1:00 – 2:30 p.m. Screening: Low Resolution, High Resilience, Selections from the Small File Media Festival. Bartos Screening Room. Free with RSVP, limited space available. 3:00 – 4:30 p.m. Small File Workshop: Introduction to Video Compression, led by Isabella Haid. Meet in MoMI Lab Classroom. Free with RSVP, limited space available. Laptops encouraged, computers will be available to those who need. So Many Things Are Not So Mark Burchick. 2024, 13 mins., 12.6 MB. United States. AN AUDIBLE MAP OF THE FIELD ON THOMAS STREET Roanna Kee. 2026, 2 mins., 2.4 MB. Ireland. Slootwater Leo Mokkola. 2024, 10 mins., 14.5 MB. Finland. Isabella Haid is an artist and researcher from Texas focused on the labor and environmental histories of computer technology. Before joining the Museum of the Moving Image, she was a Fellow at the Center for Experimental Humanities at Bard College and Visiting Researcher at the Border Tech Lab at U.T. Austin. The Small File Media Society was founded in 2020 to raise awareness of the high carbon footprint of streaming media. The festival proposes alternative solutions for media practice, as well as modes of thinking otherwise in media theory, which converged in an annual live and online festival of sustainable experimental media. The Small File team is a network of academics, researchers, curators, artists, and activists, dedicated to promoting the use of Small-File Ecomedia and the research behind it. Starting from an online festival in 2020, Small Files have found their ways into festivals, workshops, installations and panels including in Canada, Egypt, Mexico, Iran and Bangladesh.

screenings.description: Camila (Agustina Muñoz), a young Argentine theater director, travels from Buenos Aires to New York for an artistic residency where she intends to develop her new project: a new Spanish translation of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream—but upon her arrival, Camila quickly realizes that her work isn’t compensating for the loss of her friends and boyfriend she left behind. A film of quiet passion in which small gestures and objects carry great emotional weight, Hermia & Helena was the first film Piñeiro made in his adoptive home of New York City, released 10 years ago, and as such is ideally suited to screen alongside the stateside launch of his new artist’s book from Fireflies Press, From where do you start when drawing a flower?

screenings.title: Je t'aime, je t'aime
screenings.description: A “quiet mixture of science fiction with a love story as subtle as anything in Rohmer or Rivette” [Raymond Durgnat], Resnais’s definition-defying film stars Claude Rich as an unsuccessful suicide who, on leaving hospital, agrees to participate in an experiment in time travel—one that will bring fragments of his past rushing back is disordered shards.

screenings.title: The Immigrant
screenings.description: Dir. James Gray. 2014, 114 mins. U.S. DCP. With Marion Cotillard, Joaquin Phoenix, Jeremy Renner, Angela Sarafyan. Wide-eyed Ewa arrives to Ellis Island from Poland in 1921 with her sister, shivering and disoriented, and hoping to connect with her aunt in Brooklyn. Things immediately descend into confusion, and she finds herself alone on the Lower East Side, where she must scramble her way towards a new life. James Gray’s exquisitely mounted drama of New York immigrant lives at the turn of the last century forgoes period piece grandstanding in favor of finely etched authenticity. Building to an emotional crescendo of romantic sacrifice, Gray’s film, shot by the great Darius Khondji with subtle expressionism, is a hypnotic story of a woman freeing herself from subjugation as the country around her is still coming into focus. screenings.title: Force of Evil
screenings.description: Dir. Abraham Polonsky. 1948, 79 mins. U.S. DCP restored by the UCLA Film & Television Archive and The Film Foundation with funding provided by The Hobson/Lucas Family Foundation. With John Garfield, Thomas Gomez, Beatrice Pearson, Marie Windsor, Roy Roberts. A jewellike masterpiece of film noir, blacklisted director and writer Abraham Polonsky’s classic is a pure dose of moral fatalism, starring the great John Garfield as an unscrupulous Wall Street lawyer who has no qualms about getting into business with a mobster. His scheme ultimately invades the peaceful life of his more honest brother, played by Thomas Gomez. A shot to the heart of greed, this commentary on the dark effects of capitalism is an evocatively shot cornerstone of 1940s New York cinema, with a famous climax set by the George Washington Bridge. screenings.title: The Battle of Tuntenhaus
screenings.description: Juliet BashoreTHE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 1 1991, 24 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.THE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 2 1992, 19 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.“The Wall has fallen. Berlin has reunified. But there are new zones of transgression to be carved out and explored. Mainzer Straße is a hot spot of squatters and anti-fascist fights. One of the squats on this notorious street, the Tuntenhaus (‘House of Queers’), becomes a specific target of both their neo-Nazi neighbors and the iron fist of the capitalist state. Juliet Bashore’s legendary documentary follows the daily struggle of the queens and queers to create and defend a place for themselves in the chaos and unrest after the fall of communism. The extraordinary union of the anarchist/autonomous and gay scenes meets the onlooking yet involved sympathizers, who also end up in conflict with the squatters as a result of their filming. The film is a unique testimony to the violent and momentous eviction of the people from the streets.” –THE BEACONCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Suzhou River
screenings.description: Taking its name from the polluted river that flows through Shanghai, director Lou’s hometown, the brooding Suzhou River uses the singular first-person perspective of its unseen videographer-narrator to explore the grubby underbelly of the city, observing the story of an unsuspecting motorcycle courier who finds himself snared in a kidnapping plot and murder rap. A seductive, intricately structured stylistic coup from the Sixth Generation filmmaker, drawing on influences from film noir to Vertigo (1958) while developing its own idiosyncratic and haunting visual vocabulary.

screenings.title: Raging Bull
screenings.description: Dir. Martin Scorsese. 1980, 129 mins. 35mm. With Robert De Niro, Joe Pesci, Cathy Moriarty. With Raging Bull, Scorsese turned the boxing movie on its head, forgoing every cliché to create an indelible work of art. In an Oscar-winning role, De Niro is Jake La Motta, whose life story is dramatized with a mix of Shakespearean tragedy and documentary-like realism, while Pesci and Moriarty received nominations for their spectacular work as Jake’s brother and second wife. With nearly anthropological detail, Scorsese and De Niro make La Motta into the ultimate inscrutable human animal, fueled by passion and self-destruction. Michael Chapman’s glistening black-and-white cinematography is one of the glories of contemporary cinema. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. screenings.description: In their tireless search for new monsters to add to their menagerie Hammer turned here to Greek mythology, unleashing the fatal gaze of the Gorgon on the residents of a German village, c. 1910. Seven Vandorf residents have in recent years been found frozen into statuary, and it falls on the esteemed Prof. Meister of Leipzig (Christopher Lee) to overcome interference by local physician Dr. Namaroff (Peter Cushing) and track down the culprit, Megaera (ballerina-turned-film actor Prudence Hyman), a she-devil with the ability to turn flesh to stone. A small miracle of high style on a pinched budget, praised by Raymond Durgnat in Films and Filming for its “romantic warmth… with oil lamps casting a rich glow on the patchwork counterpanes and through coloured windows, and with some extraordinarily beautiful cloudscapes and dusk skies.”

screenings.description: “Poetic, political, and above all incontrovertibly material” [The New Yorker], Kogonada’s fourth feature, the experimental drama zi, follows the title character, played by Michelle Mao, a concert violinist whose aimless peregrinations through the streets of Hong Kong are interrupted by visions of what may be either her past or future, a condition she attempts to explain to a new American acquaintance (Haley Lu Richardson, Columbus) while a stranger (Jin Ha) observes the pair from a distance. A valentine to the textures and colors of the Fragrant Harbor as seen by night, featuring music by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto, the formally audacious, shot-on-the-fly zi is a film of unusual delicacy and reserve, one whose air of mystery abides long after the credits have rolled.

screenings.title: Crystal Voyager
screenings.description: Directed by Elfick, co-founder of the Australian surf magazine Tracks, “the Citizen Kane of surfing pictures” [The Guardian] follows photographer, filmmaker, and avid surfer George Greenough, as well as fellow wave-chasers Nat Young and Richie West, on a quest for secluded surf spots that goes from coastal California to Lennox Head, New South Wales, to points even further afield. A heady paean to the elements, to sun and water, whose fisheye tube-riding POV shots were received as nothing short of revolutionary when it premiered, and whose psychedelic soundtrack by The Crystal Voyager Band won it an ardent following in counterculture hot spots the world over.

screenings.title: Tripolar the Movie + Q&A
screenings.description: TRIPOLAR THE MOVIE is a biting satire disguised as a stoner comedy set in the heart of Brooklyn. Rife with John Waters-style humor, the story follows a washed-up 50-something mother and her daughter’s 20-something friends who are willing to do anything to make a film. But when a movie exec greenlights their project, they begin to conspire against one another in a parody of life in modern America.

screenings.title: White Snail
screenings.description: NEW YORK PREMIERE! FILMMAKERS IN PERSON!“Following two unconventional documentaries – SPACE DOGS (2019) and DREAMING DOGS (2024) – focused on the lives of stray canines, filmmaking duo Elsa Kremser and Levin Peter return with the narrative feature WHITE SNAIL, where the two protagonists also exhibit a fondness for various animals. Set in contemporary Belarus, the film tells the story of Masha, a blonde, thin, fair-skinned model pursuing her dream job in China, and Misha, a tattooed, thickset painter working at a morgue. Played with extreme naturalness by non-professionals Marya Imbro and Mikhail Senkov, these two loners strike up an unlikely but profound friendship that will force them to confront their secrets and wounds. The worlds to which Masha and Misha belong are completely at odds. But as these characters form a strange bond, the fashion industry and the funeral business reveal equally unlikely coincidences and areas of overlap that subtly proliferate as the plot advances. By depicting how we and our bodies relate to sight and touch, life and death, reality and imagination, flaws and perfection, Kremser and Peter map two universes on to one another, leaving the viewer to determine where they intersect and whether they diverge.” –Cristina Álvarez López, VIENNALEThese screenings are co-presented by Deutsches Haus at NYU and Erste Bank, on the occasion of the co-awarding of the 2025 Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to WHITE SNAIL. Since 2011, each annual edition of the Viennale (Vienna International FilmFestival) has featured the granting of the Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to one or more filmmakers whose films are included within the festival. Designed to showcase the best of Austrian cinema, the Award was founded by Erste Bank, the Viennale’s main sponsor, and is awarded according to the findings of an independent jury. The Award brings a cash prize as well as a residency as a visiting filmmaker organized by Deutsches Haus at NYU. Additional support for these screenings has been provided by the Austrian Cultural Forum New York.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Nina Hagen = Punk + Glory
screenings.description: Up until his untimely death earlier this year, filmmaker Peter Sempel had a long and close association with Anthology Film Archives and Jonas Mekas (about whom he made four separate feature-length film portraits over the years). In addition to his collaborations with Jonas, Sempel made numerous other experimental films and documentaries about various artists and musicians. Among his best-known works is this film about the legendary singer, songwriter, and actress Nina Hagen. Far from a conventional artist doc, NINA HAGEN = PUNK + GLORY favors spontaneous, fragmentary, and often home-movie-like glimpses of her daily life, performances, and interactions with family, friends, and colleagues (including Lemmy, George Clinton, Blixa Bargeld, Udo Kier, Dee Dee Ramone, Jonas Mekas, and others). Sempel’s goal is less to narrate Hagen’s biography than to capture her unique energy and charisma, and to shed light on her many sides, on- and off-stage.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: The third and final film of Aoyama’s “Kitakyushu Saga,” adapted from his own novel, stars Tadanobu Asano as Kenji, a young man still nursing the wounds of an unhappy childhood as he goes through the desultory motions of various odd jobs, who catches sight of an opportunity for closure—or, perhaps, revenge—when one night he recognizes the wife of one of his employers as the mother who’d abandoned him years ago, and conspires to infiltrate their household. A rich, moving human drama of families arbitrarily assigned and chosen, its large ensemble cast handled adroitly, and the proceedings given a striking, somber beauty by prodigiously gifted cinematographer Masaki Tamura.

screenings.title: Lost Highway
screenings.description: Few filmmakers have shown themselves so adept at plumbing the depths of the subconscious without coming up for air as Lynch, whose Lost Highway—inspired loosely by still-fresh coverage of the O. J. Simpson trial—begins as a dark domestic drama concerning a sexually incompetent saxophonist (Bill Pullman) and his wife (Patricia Arquette), morphs into a movie about a cocksman mechanic (Balthazar Getty) who gets involved with a gangster’s girl (Arquette, again), and ends with an unleashing of apocalyptic, purgative flame… Whether you take it as a cinematic depiction of a psychogenic fugue state or a free-associative disgorging of images from Hollywood’s id, Lynch’s film has the pull of a whirlpool and the terrible logic of a nightmare.

screenings.description: A chilling film noir like no other, Gene Tierney stars as Ellen Berent, a beautiful and possessive woman whose overly dependent love for her husband turns increasingly sinister. screenings.description: NEW YORK PREMIERE! FILMMAKERS IN PERSON!“Following two unconventional documentaries – SPACE DOGS (2019) and DREAMING DOGS (2024) – focused on the lives of stray canines, filmmaking duo Elsa Kremser and Levin Peter return with the narrative feature WHITE SNAIL, where the two protagonists also exhibit a fondness for various animals. Set in contemporary Belarus, the film tells the story of Masha, a blonde, thin, fair-skinned model pursuing her dream job in China, and Misha, a tattooed, thickset painter working at a morgue. Played with extreme naturalness by non-professionals Marya Imbro and Mikhail Senkov, these two loners strike up an unlikely but profound friendship that will force them to confront their secrets and wounds. The worlds to which Masha and Misha belong are completely at odds. But as these characters form a strange bond, the fashion industry and the funeral business reveal equally unlikely coincidences and areas of overlap that subtly proliferate as the plot advances. By depicting how we and our bodies relate to sight and touch, life and death, reality and imagination, flaws and perfection, Kremser and Peter map two universes on to one another, leaving the viewer to determine where they intersect and whether they diverge.” –Cristina Álvarez López, VIENNALEThese screenings are co-presented by Deutsches Haus at NYU and Erste Bank, on the occasion of the co-awarding of the 2025 Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to WHITE SNAIL. Since 2011, each annual edition of the Viennale (Vienna International FilmFestival) has featured the granting of the Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to one or more filmmakers whose films are included within the festival. Designed to showcase the best of Austrian cinema, the Award was founded by Erste Bank, the Viennale’s main sponsor, and is awarded according to the findings of an independent jury. The Award brings a cash prize as well as a residency as a visiting filmmaker organized by Deutsches Haus at NYU. In German with English subtitles.“The Wall has fallen. Berlin has reunified. But there are new zones of transgression to be carved out and explored. Mainzer Straße is a hot spot of squatters and anti-fascist fights. One of the squats on this notorious street, the Tuntenhaus (‘House of Queers’), becomes a specific target of both their neo-Nazi neighbors and the iron fist of the capitalist state. Juliet Bashore’s legendary documentary follows the daily struggle of the queens and queers to create and defend a place for themselves in the chaos and unrest after the fall of communism. The extraordinary union of the anarchist/autonomous and gay scenes meets the onlooking yet involved sympathizers, who also end up in conflict with the squatters as a result of their filming. The film is a unique testimony to the violent and momentous eviction of the people from the streets.” –THE BEACONCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Bitter Christmas
screenings.description: BITTER CHRISTMAS tells two alternating stories, one starring Elsa, an advertising director, in 2004, during a long weekend in December. The second takes place in 2026 and stars Raúl, a screenwriter and director who is writing a script that we soon discover is the story of Elsa, her boyfriend Bonifacio, and her friends Patricia and Natalia. Mixed with fiction, Elsa is, in a way, Raúl's alter ego, who, like him, resorts to autofiction as a solution to a long period of creative drought. He looks inside himself, and he can't help but also look at the people who make up his most intimate universe: his partner and his assistant. The film narrates the close relationship between reality and fiction, between inspiration and life, exploring the limits of autofiction and stories within stories.

screenings.title: Sneak Preview: Paper Tiger with James Gray in person
screenings.description: Dir. James Gray. 2026, 115 mins. U.S. DCP. With Adam Driver, Scarlett Johnansson, Miles Teller, Gavin Goudey, Roman Engel. Recreating a finely rendered—and personally remembered—New York of the mid 1980s, James Gray has constructed a classical moral drama of tragic proportions that is among his greatest achievements. Equal parts tender and sinister, the film stars Adam Driver as Gary Pearl, a former NYC police officer who tries to help his middle-class Queens family man brother Irving (a tremendous Miles Teller) make some extra money for wife and teenage boys by looping him in on a “sure thing” deal with some local Russians working the Gowanus Canal in Brooklyn. Of course, all doesn’t go as planned, and the film charts the mounting, fearful consequences of this get-rich-quick scheme. A deeply felt tale of loyalty and sacrifice, Paper Tiger features expressive widescreen photography and sensationally moving performances from Driver, Teller, and Johansson, who’s mesmerizing as Irving’s wife Hester, clinging to terrible secrets of her own. This is a free preview screening, courtesy of NEON. Reservations will open soon with priority given to MoMI members.

screenings.title: Postcolonial Motion: Taxis and Travelogues
screenings.description: While not as long-standing as the romance with trains, cinema has a love affair with taxis. A cab ride is often more than just a means of getting from one place to another. The taxi is a cinematic apparatus in motion, a confessional, an urban microcosm, a transition, a temporary intimacy, an archive of daily life, a nightmare of forced conversation, an eavesdropper’s dream. Yet beneath such metaphors are material threats: the gig economy, prior and enduring precarities and exploitation of labor, movements of migration conditioned by colonization.POSTCOLONIAL MOTION: TAXIS AND TRAVELOGUES draws together three films combining oral testimonies and the kinetics of transport. Frank Sweeney, Karimah Ashadu, and Timoteus Anggawan Kusno each consider the movements of people, goods and images, tracing how workers warp the barriers of historical categories and economic constraints as they cross borders.Guest-programmed by Yasmina Price, who wrote the introduction and individual film descriptions.Frank SweeneyGO YE AFAR2026, 24 min, DCPIrish research-based artist Frank Sweeney’s latest work, GO YE AFAR (2026), stages a historical examination of economy, religion, national identity, and state power through the nocturnal taxi journey of a Nigerian driver in Dublin and Calabar. Making a link between the IMF’s role in imposing a debt structure on Ireland in the 2010s and the economic dependency still inflicted on the African continent, Sweeney makes a taxi journey an illuminating lens onto the dubious legacies of Catholic missionaries and European philanthropy, global privatization and the erosion of the commons.Karimah AshaduBROWN GOODS2020, 12 min, DCPBROWN GOODS (2020), by British-born Nigerian artist and director Karimah Ashadu, both shares and reconfigures a similar terrain. The film scans the intermingled economies and geographies of Africa and Europe, conjuring Nigeria from its viewpoint in Germany. The setting is specifically Hamburg, a hub of international trade and multinational corporations. Ashadu’s agile camerawork delves through docks, weaving amongst ship containers and stacks of tires as Emeka – the self-sufficient central figure, excluded from formal work due to his humanitarian status – voices a sharp analysis of manufacturing and industrial monopolies, the politics of resources and global capital.Timoteus Anggawan KusnoOBSCURA2026, 14 min, DCPIndonesian filmmaker and visual artist Timoteus Anggawan Kusno’s OBSCURA (2026) echoes the unsettling, spectral dreaminess and mediatized archival memory of GO YE AFAR. Operating between Indonesia and the Netherlands, the film critically reworks the form of the ethnographic travelogue and colonial imagery through a story of theft (another kind of informal job). Gallery workers liberate a painting and carry it out in a truck, performing how images physically travel, are taken apart, literally unframed and reframed.Total running time: ca. 55 min.The screening will be followed by a conversation with filmmaker and artist Frank Sweeney!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: Shortly before the 1973 Chilean coup, CIA agents Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell) are dispatched from Santiago to Easter island by their bureau chief, MJ (Steve Buscemi). screenings.title: Narrow Rooms: Drunken Noodles
screenings.description: Lucio CastroDRUNKEN NOODLES2025, 83 min, DCP. In English and Spanish with English subtitles.When Adnan (Laith Khalifeh) arrives in New York to work at a Lower East Side gallery for the summer, he’s newly single and ready to mingle. He cruises strangers in the park at night and begins a flirtation with a delivery driver. At work, he’s helping to exhibit the recently discovered work of Sal Salandra, a real-world gay artist and elder who crafts tableaus of gay orgies and sex club scenes in vibrant needlepoint. These artworks – and Sal himself, played by Ezriel Kornel – become the connective thread for a time-jumping narrative that unfolds in four parts. Made for little money, with a small crew and total creative control, the latest by Lucio Castro (END OF THE CENTURY) is a delightful, sexually-charged short-story collection with whimsical elements of dreamy magical realism. Released during the full flower of NYC PRIDE season, DRUNKEN NOODLES is well worth watching – or rewatching – before making your Best-of-2026 lists.We’ll be joined by director Lucio Castro and cast members for a Q&A following the screening!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Bitter Christmas
screenings.description: BITTER CHRISTMAS tells two alternating stories, one starring Elsa, an advertising director, in 2004, during a long weekend in December. The second takes place in 2026 and stars Raúl, a screenwriter and director who is writing a script that we soon discover is the story of Elsa, her boyfriend Bonifacio, and her friends Patricia and Natalia. Mixed with fiction, Elsa is, in a way, Raúl's alter ego, who, like him, resorts to autofiction as a solution to a long period of creative drought. He looks inside himself, and he can't help but also look at the people who make up his most intimate universe: his partner and his assistant. The film narrates the close relationship between reality and fiction, between inspiration and life, exploring the limits of autofiction and stories within stories.

screenings.title: The Killing of a Sacred Deer
screenings.description: The year before enjoying enormous popular success with The Favourite, Lanthimos rolled out perhaps his most difficult and disquieting film to date, a Greek tragedy transplanted to the American suburbs starring Colin Farrell as Steven Murphy, a cardiothoracic surgeon who opens his home in an unguarded moment to a fatherless 16-year-old (Barry Keoghan)… and, as it happens, to a terrible retribution that threatens Murphy’s wife (Nicole Kidman), teenaged daughter, and adolescent son. “A typically arch dramatic conundrum, laced with Lanthimos’s trademark off-kilter artifice and deadpan humour… An increasingly sickening hunger game driven by an inflexible moral imperative.” —The Observer

screenings.title: zi
screenings.description: “Poetic, political, and above all incontrovertibly material” [The New Yorker], Kogonada’s fourth feature, the experimental drama zi, follows the title character, played by Michelle Mao, a concert violinist whose aimless peregrinations through the streets of Hong Kong are interrupted by visions of what may be either her past or future, a condition she attempts to explain to a new American acquaintance (Haley Lu Richardson, Columbus) while a stranger (Jin Ha) observes the pair from a distance. A valentine to the textures and colors of the Fragrant Harbor as seen by night, featuring music by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto, the formally audacious, shot-on-the-fly zi is a film of unusual delicacy and reserve, one whose air of mystery abides long after the credits have rolled.

screenings.title: Je t'aime, je t'aime
screenings.description: A “quiet mixture of science fiction with a love story as subtle as anything in Rohmer or Rivette” [Raymond Durgnat], Resnais’s definition-defying film stars Claude Rich as an unsuccessful suicide who, on leaving hospital, agrees to participate in an experiment in time travel—one that will bring fragments of his past rushing back is disordered shards.

screenings.title: Barbara
screenings.description: With Jeanne Balibar, Mathieu Amalric, Vincent Peirani, Aurore Clement, and Grégoire Colin.Amalric’s seventh feature-length film as a director is both a heartfelt tribute to the legendary chanteuse Barbara (1930-97), and a vehicle for another peerlessly talented French luminary, the actress and singer Jeanne Balibar. Amalric’s films are remarkable for their intuitive freedom, and their emphasis on emotional textures and states of feeling rather than on straightforward narrative construction or easily grasped meanings. BARBARA is a case in point: eschewing anything like a coherent, birth-to-death account of the events of her life, the film instead orchestrates fragments of the singer’s life and performances into a free and quasi-abstract meditation on Barbara’s identity and cultural presence. And by casting Balibar not as Barbara per se but more self-referentially as an actress making a film-within-the-film about the singer, his film becomes an even broader investigation into the concept of biographical filmmaking, representation, and identity. An experimental biopic in the tradition of Stanley Kwan’s CENTER STAGE, Peter Watkins’s EDVARD MUNCH, and Paul Leduc’s FRIDA, it features a typically riveting, charismatic performance from Balibar.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Playback
screenings.description: On the edge of his 40th birthday Haji (Jun Murakami), an actor haunted by dreams of his own death, accepts an invitation from an old friend to revisit his hometown for a wedding—only to doze off en route and wake to find himself in the school uniform of his youth, seemingly catapulted back into the past. A remarkably mature, circumspect depiction of middle-age morass and melancholia from a director who was only in his mid-twenties when he made it, Playback’s premiere at the 2012 Locarno Film Festival established Miyake as a filmmaker to watch. A work of bold experimentation and teasing ambiguity, described by his friend Ryusuke Hamaguchi as “like a modern-day reincarnation of [John Cassavetes’s] Opening Night.”

screenings.title: Harakiri, I Miss You + Q&A
screenings.description: Three young friends wander through Madrid over 24 hours, tangled in rivalry and fragile masculinity. Obsessed with an older woman who teases and rejects them, they face encounters that push them to the edge—a raw portrait of youth lost between desire and emotional violence.

screenings.title: Cabaret
screenings.description: Dir. Bob Fosse. 1972, 124 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Liza Minnelli, Michael York, Helmut Griem, Joel Grey, Maria Berenson. Fosse rightly won the Best Director Oscar for his shattering musical set in Berlin on the eve of Hitler’s rise to power. Liza Minnelli and Joel Grey also scored Oscars for their unforgettable performances as, respectively, Sally Bowles, a vivacious but damaged American singer selling her soul in a seedy nightclub, and the devilish emcee who presides over it. A devastating, delirious movie experience, featuring John Kander and Fred Ebb’s rousing show tunes and Geoffrey Unsworth’s gloriously ragged photography, Cabaret reinvented the movie musical for 1970s American cinema and all but wrote a new cinematic grammar for how to shoot and edit song and dance. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: In Bed with Victoria
screenings.description: High-powered lawyer Victoria (Efira) is an unstoppable force in the courtroom, but off the clock she struggles to raise her two daughters on her own, respond to the latest online defamation from her vindictive ex-husband, and feign more than passing interest in her latest app-arranged fuck-and-run. While wrapped up in a singularly unusual case brought to her by an old pal (Melvil Poupaud), Victoria reconnects with a onetime client (Vincent Lacoste) who seems to offer the prospect of something more than a desultory fling… that is, if she’s ready or able to accept what’s on offer. A frisky, funny showcase for Efira, unforgettable as the pouty, rumpled, restless, reckless Victoria, smart and savvy in its upending of rom-com cliché.

screenings.title: Crystal Voyager
screenings.description: Directed by Elfick, co-founder of the Australian surf magazine Tracks, “the Citizen Kane of surfing pictures” [The Guardian] follows photographer, filmmaker, and avid surfer George Greenough, as well as fellow wave-chasers Nat Young and Richie West, on a quest for secluded surf spots that goes from coastal California to Lennox Head, New South Wales, to points even further afield. A heady paean to the elements, to sun and water, whose fisheye tube-riding POV shots were received as nothing short of revolutionary when it premiered, and whose psychedelic soundtrack by The Crystal Voyager Band won it an ardent following in counterculture hot spots the world over.

screenings.title: The Landlord | The Ravishing Cinema of Bill Gunn
screenings.description: Written by visionary black filmmaker Bill Gunn and the first film of Oscar-winning director Hal Ashby, The Landlord is both a coming-of-age tale and a social satire. When wealthy, white Elger Winthrop Enders buys a tenement brownstone in pre-gentrified Park Slope Brooklyn, he plans to evict its predominantly Black residents. Instead, he becomes entangled in the lives of his tenants.

screenings.title: Tenebrae
screenings.description: Argento’s return to his giallo roots after veering off into gonzo horror/fantasy, Tenebrae features Anthony Franciosa as an American author of potboiler thrillers who, promoting a new book in Rome, finds that a murderer is re-enacting his most ghoulish delights of literary fancy. Argento uses the occasion to scale new, dizzying heights of his own, employing bravura crane shots, brazenly baroque lighting, and the iconic moment of a razor slashing through white cotton.

screenings.title: Drive
screenings.description: Drawing inspiration from Walter Hill’s The Driver, Refn’s high-style tour-de-force stars Ryan Gosling as a loner Los Angeles stunt driver who moonlights as a getaway wheelman on armed stickups, who’s put on a collision course with a nefarious criminal syndicate thanks to his protective affection for neighbor Carey Mulligan. A terse, tough, and morosely moody film propelled by a shimmering synth-pop score, with an extraordinary supporting cast that includes an against-type Albert Brooks as a sullen, profane gangster kingpin.

screenings.title: Les rendez-vous d'Anna
screenings.description: Akerman’s third feature was this transfixing—and, one suspects, quite personal—study of alienation and emotional withdrawal, in which a well-known Belgian director (Aurore Clément), traveling the increasingly homogenized cities of Western Europe to promote her latest movie, eavesdrops on conversations and passes through a series of brief encounters with acquaintances old and new, including a one-night stand with Helmut Griem, a reconnection with ex-lover Jean-Pierre Cassel, and a stiff reception from aloof mother Lea Massari.

screenings.title: The Souvenir
screenings.description: Hogg, who has quietly established herself as one of the finest UK filmmakers working, offers a keenly observed, sometimes bruising portrayal of toxic romance set in ’80s Britain, starring Honor Swinton Byrne (daughter of Tilda, who plays the character’s patrician mother) as Julie, an aspiring filmmaker who begins a relationship with Anthony (Tom Burke), a slightly older man in the employ of the Foreign Office whose attractive intelligence and worldliness can’t compensate for the fact that he is an addict and a natural manipulator. Hogg’s usual compositional rigor works in service of enormously empathic semi-autobiographical storytelling, using flashback inserts in order to plumb the psychology of a hopelessly dysfunctional relationship.

screenings.title: Some Came Running
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1958, 137 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Frank Sinatra, Shirley MacLaine, Dean Martin, Martha Hyer, Arthur Kennedy. Minnelli’s phenomenally directed and acted tale of rootlessness in post–World War II America stars Frank Sinatra as a war veteran and former writer who has fallen into alcoholism, and who returns to his Indiana hometown to find nothing is quite as he remembered it. Dean Martin is the unrepentant gambler whom he befriends, and Shirley MacLaine is heartbreaking in a signature early role as a wayward woman who limps after him, hoping he will love her. One of the great American melodramas of the 1950s, this CinemaScope adaptation of James Jones’s novel builds to a frenetic carnival climax that is among Minnelli’s finest achievements. screenings.title: 16mm Cartoons: Raunchy, Sexy & Risqué + Q&A
screenings.description: Back in the ‘pre-code’ era of the 1920s and early 1930s, animated cartoons were made to entertain the adults in the audience. The results were often sexually suggestive, if not borderline explicit. Much later, with the long overdue relaxation of old censorship codes, independent and experimental animators of the 1960s and beyond became free to openly explore the raunchy and risqué once more. Salacious sexiness, lustful adultery, queerness, Peeping Toms, and other questionable—or perfectly human—adult behaviors were only some of the wonderfully ‘vulgar’ themes present in animated shorts made in both eras.

screenings.title: Shutter Island
screenings.description: An infamous triple filicide has escaped from Ashecliffe Hospital, located on a rugged islet in Boston Harbor that bears a striking resemblance to Arnold Böcklin’s Island of the Dead, and US Marshal Chuck Aule and his new partner (Leonardo DiCaprio and Mark Ruffalo) are on the scene to investigate. Set in the postwar period that gave birth to some of the most anguished of all film noir, Scorsese’s feverish thriller is awash in the psychic trauma of the mid-century, its soundtrack a catalog of jarring modernist classical compiled by collaborator Robbie Robertson and including work by Krzysztof Penderecki, John Cage, and Max Richter, among others, with Robert Richardson’s cinematography suggesting a particularly jaundiced, blighted version of the Technicolor process.

screenings.title: And Your Bird Can Sing preceded by August 8th
screenings.description: “Among Sho Miyake's most quietly luminous works, And Your Bird Can Sing is a tender and deeply felt portrait of youth poised between freedom and uncertainty. Adapted from Yasushi Sato's novel and set in the port city of Hakodate, the film follows three young adults drifting through work, friendship, and desire as summer gives way to an uncertain future. With its naturalistic performances, loose rhythms, and extraordinary sensitivity to time, place, and everyday gestures, Miyake finds profound emotional resonance in the ordinary, affirming his distinctive voice in contemporary Japanese cinema.” —Shun Inoue, Japan Foundation

screenings.title: Leave Her to Heaven
screenings.description: A chilling film noir like no other, Gene Tierney stars as Ellen Berent, a beautiful and possessive woman whose overly dependent love for her husband turns increasingly sinister. Shot in gorgeous technicolor by director John M. Stahl and DP Leon Shamroy (winner of the Academy Award for Best Color Cinematography), Leave Her to Heaven became 20th Century Fox’s highest-grossing film of the 1940’s. At the rotten center is an Oscar-nominated performance from Tierney, playing the rare femme fatale who isn’t motivated by all-American greed and ambition, but instead is consumed by obsession, jealousy, and deadly devotion.

screenings.title: Music Is Music + Before It’s Too Late
The French Connection
screenings.description: Dir. William Friedkin. 1971, 104 mins. DCP. With Gene Hackman, Roy Scheider, Fernando Rey, Tony Lo Bianco. “I felt this was a kind of crude poem to the city,” said director William Friedkin about this emotionally complex action masterpiece about an ethically dubious New York City cop, “Popeye” Doyle, who will do anything to take down a ring of foreign heroin smugglers. The justly celebrated car and elevated subway chase through Bensonhurst required an actual Transit Authority motorman on set and five weeks to complete. Friedkin’s breakthrough won Best Picture and four other Oscars, including Gene Hackman for Best Actor. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. screenings.title: American Baby + Q&A
screenings.description: American Baby follows Oli as she navigates the repercussions of being very young and very pregnant in small-town Texas. As she seeks out the suddenly absent teenage father-to-be of her child, Oli confronts the growing isolation from her community.

screenings.title: Ec: Intolerance
screenings.description: Griffith’s immensely influential silent epic intercuts four parallel tales from history (spanning Babylon, Christ’s Judea, Reformation Europe, and turn-of-the-century America) to embroider a moral tapestry on personal, social, and political repression through the ages. The visual poetry is overwhelming, especially in the massed crowd scenes, and the unbridled eroticism of the Babylon harem scenes demonstrates just what Hollywood lost when it later bowed to the Hays Code. While the (partly self-financed) production ruined Griffith financially and baffled audiences with its multiple plots and labyrinthine structure, it has been enormously influential on generations of filmmakers, including Eisenstein, who studied the film closely.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: All the Long Nights
screenings.description: Based on the novel of the same name by Maiko Seo, Miyake’s tender, understated drama stars Hokuto Matsumura and Mone Kamishiraishi as two co-workers who, after discovering they both suffer from invisibly debilitating conditions little understood by the wider world—he from blindsiding panic attacks, she from wild PMS-related mood swings—form a tentative bond based on mutual respect and care. Often affecting but never given to unearned sentiment, abhorrent of cliché, caricature, and easy scapegoating, All The Long Nights is a deeply humane film about the everyday hurdles faced in muddling through life, buoyed by the considerable chemistry of its irresistible leads.

screenings.title: Slither
screenings.description: No sooner has car thief Dick Kanipsia (James Caan) been sprung from the pen than he finds himself in hot water all over again, set out on the trail of a cache of stolen loot, tangled up with a freewheeling chick with a penchant for armed robbery (Sally Kellerman) and a bush-league bandleader (Peter Boyle), and trying to keep ahead of a an Airstream trailer full of bad news…

screenings.title: Dr. Strangelove Or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1964. 95 mins. 35mm. With Peter Sellers, George C. Scott, Sterling Hayden, Slim Pickens, Keenan Wynn. Stanley Kubrick reinvents the nuclear suspense thriller, then in vogue, as an absurdist black comedy in this brilliant evocation of cold war paranoia. Dr. Strangelove, co-written by Kubrick and Terry Southern, strikes just the right manic, irreverent, sexually charged tone, creating a satirical masterpiece that is one of the seminal counterculture works of the 1960s. Towering over the cast—which also includes George C. Scott as the blustering General Buck Turgidson and Sterling Hayden as “precious bodily fluids”–obsessed General Jack D. Ripper—is Sellers, a triple threat as meek RAF Captain Mandrake, bungling U.S. President Merkin Muffley, and, of course, the mad scientist title character—inventor of the doomsday machine that may wipe out humanity as we know it. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. screenings.title: The Landlord | The Ravishing Cinema of Bill Gunn
screenings.description: Written by visionary black filmmaker Bill Gunn and the first film of Oscar-winning director Hal Ashby, The Landlord is both a coming-of-age tale and a social satire. When wealthy, white Elger Winthrop Enders buys a tenement brownstone in pre-gentrified Park Slope Brooklyn, he plans to evict its predominantly Black residents. Instead, he becomes entangled in the lives of his tenants.

screenings.title: The State of Things
screenings.description: German filmmaker Friedrich (Patrick Bauchau) is holed up at a hotel on the storm-lashed Portuguese coast, using American funding to shoot a shoestring budget post-apocalyptic thriller, though mostly he winds up playing a waiting game with cast and crew (including Warhol star Viva, Sam Fuller, Isabelle Weingarten, and co-writer Robert Kramer) after their producer disappears without a trace. An intermediate production made during the difficult shoot of Wenders’s 1982 Hammett for Francis Ford Coppola’s Zoetrope Studios in the US, sumptuously shot in black and white by legendary DP Henri Alekan, The State of Things is Wenders’s meditation on the complicated co-dependence of the European and American film industries.

screenings.title: The Killing of a Sacred Deer
screenings.description: The year before enjoying enormous popular success with The Favourite, Lanthimos rolled out perhaps his most difficult and disquieting film to date, a Greek tragedy transplanted to the American suburbs starring Colin Farrell as Steven Murphy, a cardiothoracic surgeon who opens his home in an unguarded moment to a fatherless 16-year-old (Barry Keoghan)… and, as it happens, to a terrible retribution that threatens Murphy’s wife (Nicole Kidman), teenaged daughter, and adolescent son. “A typically arch dramatic conundrum, laced with Lanthimos’s trademark off-kilter artifice and deadpan humour… An increasingly sickening hunger game driven by an inflexible moral imperative.” —The Observer

screenings.title: Ec: Eggeling / Grant / Jacobs & Fleischner
screenings.description: Viking EggelingSYMPHONIE DIAGONALE (1924, 8 min, 35mm, silent)“This early experimental short is one of only two films completed by Swedish-born artist Viking Eggeling, who worked in Paris, Milan, and ultimately Germany. It utilizes paper cutouts, tin foil, and frame-by-frame photography to create a playful show in which cubist, even art deco, circles and lines dance – diagonally – across the black screen.” –FACETSDwinell GrantCOMPOSITION #2 CONTRATHEMIS (1941, 5 min, 16mm, silent)“An attempt to develop visual abstract themes and to counterpoint them in a planned, formal composition.” –Dwinell GrantSTOP MOTION TESTS (1942, 3 min, 16mm, silent)A pixillated self-portrait of the filmmaker in his studio.COLOR SEQUENCE (1943, 3 min, 16mm, silent)“Pure solid-color frames which fade, mutate and flicker. A research into color rhythms and perceptual phenomena.” –William MoritzKen Jacobs & Bob FleischnerBLONDE COBRA1959-63, 35 min, 16mm-to-35mm blow-up. With Jack Smith. Preserved by Anthology Film Archives with support from The Film Foundation.“BLONDE COBRA is an erratic narrative – no, not really a narrative, it’s only stretched out in time for convenience of delivery. It’s a look in on an exploding life, on a man of imagination suffering pre-fashionable Lower East Side deprivation and consumed with American 1950s, 40s, 30s disgust. Silly, self-pitying, guilt-strictured and yet triumphing – on one level – over the situation with style… enticing us into an absurd moral posture the better to dismiss us with a regal ‘screw off.’” –Ken JacobsTotal running time: ca. 60 min.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Harakiri, I Miss You + Q&A
screenings.description: Three young friends wander through Madrid over 24 hours, tangled in rivalry and fragile masculinity. Obsessed with an older woman who teases and rejects them, they face encounters that push them to the edge—a raw portrait of youth lost between desire and emotional violence.

screenings.title: Lost Highway
screenings.description: Few filmmakers have shown themselves so adept at plumbing the depths of the subconscious without coming up for air as Lynch, whose Lost Highway—inspired loosely by still-fresh coverage of the O. J. Simpson trial—begins as a dark domestic drama concerning a sexually incompetent saxophonist (Bill Pullman) and his wife (Patricia Arquette), morphs into a movie about a cocksman mechanic (Balthazar Getty) who gets involved with a gangster’s girl (Arquette, again), and ends with an unleashing of apocalyptic, purgative flame… Whether you take it as a cinematic depiction of a psychogenic fugue state or a free-associative disgorging of images from Hollywood’s id, Lynch’s film has the pull of a whirlpool and the terrible logic of a nightmare.

screenings.title: The Brood
screenings.description: In The Brood, the bitter divorce between the mentally disturbed Nola (Samantha Eggar) and her ex-husband Frank (Art Hindle) was pretty messy, so it should be a good sign that she’s finally getting professional help from the renowned Dr. Hal Raglan (Oliver Reed)—but Frank can’t help but notice that people on Nola’s long list of enemies keep dying at the hands of asexual, dwarfish assassins, and so he starts to wonder what exactly the experimental therapy practiced at Dr. Raglan’s Somafree Institute consists of… Written while Cronenberg was in the midst of his own divorce and custody battle, The Brood is a brutal, bracing airing of anxieties gussied up in grindhouse trappings.

screenings.title: zi
screenings.description: “Poetic, political, and above all incontrovertibly material” [The New Yorker], Kogonada’s fourth feature, the experimental drama zi, follows the title character, played by Michelle Mao, a concert violinist whose aimless peregrinations through the streets of Hong Kong are interrupted by visions of what may be either her past or future, a condition she attempts to explain to a new American acquaintance (Haley Lu Richardson, Columbus) while a stranger (Jin Ha) observes the pair from a distance. A valentine to the textures and colors of the Fragrant Harbor as seen by night, featuring music by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto, the formally audacious, shot-on-the-fly zi is a film of unusual delicacy and reserve, one whose air of mystery abides long after the credits have rolled.

screenings.title: Wallace & Gromit: The Classic Shorts
screenings.description: Along with the Academy Award–winning success of Aardman Animations’ 1990 Creature Comforts, it was this trio of inspired shorts featuring cheese-loving, jug-eared, Wigan-based crackpot inventor Wallace and his erudite pet dog/straight man/frequent savior Gromit that established the company as a stop-motion dynasty to delight all ages. Featuring A Grand Day Out, in which Wallace whips up a homemade spaceship in order to sample lunar cheddar; The Wrong Trousers, in which nefarious penguin Feathers McGraw employs a new Wallace patent in a daring heist; and A Close Shave, in which our heroes must step away from their window washing concern to foil a sheep rustling operation.

screenings.title: The Long, Long Trailer
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1953, 96 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Lucille Ball, Desi Arnaz, Marjorie Main, Keenan Wynn. Lucy and Desi and Minnelli? Talk about a dream team. In this hilarious mix of romantic comedy, slapstick, and suspense, Ball and Arnaz—at the time the two most popular performers in the nation—play Tacy and Nicky (of course), an engaged couple who purchase a trailer so they can journey the country and play at domesticity before tying the knot. Aside from getting to see America’s favorite redhead in Technicolor, The Long, Long Trailer, the only major big-screen outing for the TV icons, offers up the perfect premise for a 1950s comedy, commenting on the comforts of postwar material culture with escalating madcap brilliance. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. screenings.title: Benedetta
screenings.description: Inspired by the life of Benedetta Carlini, a nun of 17th-century Tuscany whose claims of mystic visions drew the attention of church higher-ups, their investigations eventually revealing a verboten sexual relationship between Carlini and one of her fellow nuns and leading to her imprisonment, Verhoeven’s earthy, irreverent film immerses one in the squelchy squalor and earthly delights of Counter-Reformation era Europe, with Virginie Efira a revelation in the title role and Charlotte Rampling, as the abbess of the convent, conveying roiling inner turmoil beneath a cooly composed exterior. An examination of the difficult relationship between religious submission and sexual liberation, featuring some of the most memorable foley sounds in recent cinema.

screenings.title: The Souvenir
screenings.description: Hogg, who has quietly established herself as one of the finest UK filmmakers working, offers a keenly observed, sometimes bruising portrayal of toxic romance set in ’80s Britain, starring Honor Swinton Byrne (daughter of Tilda, who plays the character’s patrician mother) as Julie, an aspiring filmmaker who begins a relationship with Anthony (Tom Burke), a slightly older man in the employ of the Foreign Office whose attractive intelligence and worldliness can’t compensate for the fact that he is an addict and a natural manipulator. Hogg’s usual compositional rigor works in service of enormously empathic semi-autobiographical storytelling, using flashback inserts in order to plumb the psychology of a hopelessly dysfunctional relationship.

screenings.title: Losing Ground | The Ravishing Cinema of Bill Gunn
screenings.description: The inimitable Kathleen Collins’s second film tells the story of two remarkable people, married and hurtling toward a crossroads in their lives: Sara Rogers, a Black professor of philosophy, is embarking on an intellectual quest just as her painter husband, Victor, sets off on an exploration of joy. Victor decides to rent a country house away from the city, but the couple’s summer idyll becomes complicated by his involvement with a younger model. One of the very first fictional features by an African-American woman, Losing Ground remains a stunning and powerful work of art for being a funny, brilliant, and personal member of indie cinema canon.

screenings.title: Maîtres Anciens – Comédie
screenings.description: “Like Reger – the character [Austrian novelist and playwright] Thomas Bernhard placed on a museum bench facing a painting by Tintoretto, an ‘Old Master’ if ever there was one – an actor finds himself alone and thwarted after a notorious virus forces the indefinite closure of theaters. He wanders through an empty auditorium, paces the now-useless backstage areas, and bursts out into a street haunted by masked passersby. Having persuaded a firefighter to keep watch over him and his explosives, he pours out – to the guard and the surrounding silence alike – his loathing for, among other things, Heideggerians, a lack of punctuality, people who admire rather than respect, and the State’s appropriation of children. At the intersection of cinema and theater, despair and the will to survive, 1980s Austria and 2020s France, Bernhard’s text takes on a new resonance: ‘And as for culture in this country, your stomach exists only to turn.’” –Marie Hermann, FIDMarseillePreceded by:Mathieu Amalric C’EST PRESQUE AU BOUT DU MONDE (2015, 16 min, digital. With Barbara Hannigan.)“In C’EST PRESQUE AU BOUT DU MONDE, I explore a mystery that fascinates me: where do these inhuman voices come from? From where in the body does the unsettling anomaly of singing originate?” –Mathieu AmalricTotal running time: ca. 100 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Somewhere in the Night
screenings.description: Mankiewicz’s sophomore effort as director was this sinisterly atmospheric, baroquely plotted, deliriously disorienting “nervous nightmare” [The Village Voice] starring John Hodiak as an amnesiac ex-Marine who returns to his native Los Angeles to trawl its nightclubs, sanitariums, and docks in search of clues to his identity and traces of a mysterious stranger by the name of “Larry Cravat.” It’s a mission that puts him in close contact with the criminal underworld and a rogue’s gallery of unusual characters (Richard Conte, Josephine Hutchinson, and Fritz Kortner are on-hand in piquant supporting parts) while tying him up in a hunt for Nazi-plundered treasure.

screenings.title: Lorraine O'Grady: Rivers, First Draft Performance
screenings.description: “Rivers, First Draft was a one-time only performance created by O’Grady for Art Across the Park, curated by Gilbert Coker and Horace Brockington. It was performed in the Loch, a northern section of Central Park, on August 18, 1982, as a ‘collage-in-space,’ with different actions taking place simultaneously on two sides of the stream and further up the hill. Competing for attention, the two narratives are about uniting different heritages—the Caribbean and New England—and three different ages and aspects of the self: a young girl, a teenager, and an adult woman. It’s a three-ring circus of movement and sound that, unlike the randomness of Futurists attempting to shout each other down, plays more like a unitary dream. Preceded by Meeting Lorraine O’Grady, a short film in which multi-hyphenate talent Ashton visits O’Grady at her home in New York City, where they discuss race, gender, and the challenges for Black women artists in an often-segregated art world. Ashton and O’Grady also visit the site in Central Park where O’Grady performed Rivers First Draft.” —Robert Ransick, Executive Director & Trustee, Lorraine O’Grady Trust

screenings.title: The Cobweb
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1955, 134 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Lauren Bacall, Richard Widmark, Gloria Grahame, Lillian Gish, Charles Boyer, John Kerr, Susan Strasberg, Oscar Levant. An essential Minnelli, featuring maybe his most wildly stacked cast, The Cobweb confidently offers up a nearly undefinable mix of the restrained and the truly eccentric. Set in a psychiatric hospital, where the staff is likely more unsettled than the patients, this Cinemascope, Eastmancolor contraption details the fallout after the head doctor’s wife does the unthinkable: she changes the color of the library’s drapes! Long read as a perfect auteur text for Minnelli (who got his start as a window dresser), The Cobweb is a gorgeously shot, low-boil soap opera that’s a must for any 1950s melodrama completist. screenings.title: Ec: Une Simple Histoire
screenings.description: “Based on a true incident, the film chronicles the wanderings of a woman and child looking for work and lodging in Paris. This is the only plot, and Hanoun has little interest in embellishing it with background and motivation: he never even makes it clear, for example, whether the woman is the child’s mother, guardian or companion. UNE SIMPLE HISTOIRE is, more than a narrative, a formal stylistic exercise so rigorously disciplined and understated that it makes the visual asceticism of Robert Bresson seem almost Fellini-esque by comparison.” –TIMECLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: After her divisive debut feature, Anne, an up-and-coming filmmaker, sets out to make her sophomore film, In Memory of Anne Heche. However things quickly take a turn for the worse as scenes go awry, actors drop out, and Anne’s prickly friendship with her lead actress becomes increasingly toxic.

screenings.title: The Woman on the Beach
screenings.description: Though mutilated by RKO Pictures following a disastrous test screening, Renoir’s final Hollywood feature remains a film unlike any in its director’s filmography—not to speak of contemporary American cinema—a marvel of brooding atmosphere in which a Coast Guard officer haunted by the memory of a maritime tragedy (Robert Ryan), recently engaged, is bewitched by a dark beauty (Joan Bennett), the wife of a blind painter, whom he meets while riding at seaside, his attraction to her by no means unrequited. A disarmingly frank depiction of consuming, destructive erotic obsession, with a roiling, elemental score by Hanns Eisler contributing to the palpable sense of gathering doom.

screenings.title: The Cockpit
screenings.description: The “cockpit” of the title is a cramped apartment in the suburbs of Tokyo, unprepossessing in size but bursting with creative ferment, for this dinky flat is functioning as the recording studio where underground producer-rapper OMSB and cohort Bim are laying down a new track, to be titled “Curve Death Match.” Shot largely from a camera locked down to the workstation and facing the duo, The Cockpit follows the songwriting process from sampling to beat-making to writing to the final recording, in the process giving an intimate, pared-to-the-bone, nuts-and-bolts breakdown of the intricacies of hip-hop artistry without rival.

screenings.title: Ec: Jerome Hill
screenings.description: These 35mm prints are the result of a preservation project undertaken by the Museum of Modern Art.DEATH IN THE FORENOON (1934/66, 2 min, 35mm)CANARIES (1969, 4 min, 35mm)&FILM PORTRAIT(1971, 81 min, 35mm)“FILM PORTRAIT is an autobiography in the sense that it deals explicitly with Jerome’s most personal life’s relationship to film. It draws on film clips taken in his childhood and his whole childhood involvement in art and life. It comes closest to any kind of filmic answer to Proust. […] FILM PORTRAIT is, I believe, the only direct autobiography we have in film. There is Jonas Mekas’s WALDEN, which is diary but not autobiography in a strict sense. We have Cocteau’s BLOOD OF A POET, ORPHEUS, and TESTAMENT OF ORPHEUS. One could say that this last is autobiographical, but it is also allusive and poetic; whereas Jerome’s FILM PORTRAIT is a very straight attempt to present autobiography on film. Of course, subsequently, James Broughton’s TESTAMENT and my own SINCERITY & DUPLICITY series of autobiographical films were very much inspired by Jerome’s FILM PORTRAIT as well as by Jonas’s WALDEN. […] Jerome Hill’s films are great because they are poised on wit and achieve a balance – a gentle, intentional, particularly American balance.” –Stan Brakhage, FILM AT WIT’S ENDTotal running time: ca. 90 min.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Celebration
screenings.description: The opening salvo in Dogme 95’s all-out assault on cinematic artifice, revolutionary in its emancipated use of the Sony DCR-PC7 Handycam, Vinterberg’s scorched earth melodrama/farce takes place during a gathering of the extended Hansen clan at a family-run hotel to mark the 60th birthday of solid burgher patriarch Helge (Henning Moritzen)—an event that takes a turn for the chaotic when Helge’s eldest son, Christian (Ulrich Thomsen), accuses his father of molesting both himself and his recently deceased twin sister during a dinner table toast. Abrasive, volatile, savagely funny, and endlessly inventive, one can scarcely feel indifferent towards such a blood-on-the-walls affair as this.

screenings.title: Detour
screenings.description: Hearing a certain tune spin on the jukebox in an all-night diner in Reno sends down-on-his-luck pianist Al Roberts (Tom Neal) on a traumatic trip down memory lane, recalling his fateful roadside encounter with Ann Savage’s aptly named femme fatale Vera and his subsequent subjugation to her, in Ulmer’s made-for-peanuts classic of noir absurdism, one of the priceless treasures to emerge from Hollywood’s so-called “Poverty Row” studios. “Possibly the bleakest, most doom-laden film noir ever… Savage’s sensational performance, combined with the real-life trajectory of Neal, who ended up going to prison for murdering his wife, have made this a tormented film with the despairing logic of nightmare.” —The Los Angeles Times

screenings.title: Ec: Hugo / Jacobs / Levitt / Maas
screenings.description: Ian HugoBELLS OF ATLANTIS(1952, 10 min, 16mm. Preserved by the Library of Congress through the Avant-Garde Masters program funded by The Film Foundation and administered by the National Film Preservation Foundation.)A film poem, based on Anaïs Nin’s HOUSE OF INCEST, narrated by and featuring Nin.“[BELLS OF ATLANTIS was] inspired by the prologue to my HOUSE OF INCEST and the line: ‘I remember my first birth in water.’ The film evoked the watery depths of the lost continent of Atlantis. It is a lyrical journey into prenatal memories, the theme of birth and rebirth from the sea.” –Anaïs NinKen JacobsLITTLE STABS AT HAPPINESS (1959-63, 18 min, 16mm. With Jack Smith.)“Material was cut in as it came out of the camera, embarrassing moments intact. 100’ rolls timed well with music on old 78s. I was interested in immediacy, a sense of ease, and an art where suffering was acknowledged but not trivialized with dramatics. Whimsy was our achievement, as well as breaking out of step.” –Ken JacobsHelen Levitt, Janice Loeb, and James AgeeIN THE STREET (1952, 12 min, 16mm, silent. Preserved by Anthology Film Archives.)“Informality is indeed the crucial and virtually definitive quality of IN THE STREET; it is even the guiding principle and vision. […] This is the extreme realization of a classic ‘naturalistic’ genre, the German ‘street film,’ where the street was imaged as the arena of the everyday and random, the channel in which the ‘stream of life’ conveniently became microcosmic.” –Ken Kelman, THE ESSENTIAL CINEMAWillard MaasGEOGRAPHY OF THE BODY (1943, 7 min, 16mm, b&w. Preserved by Anthology with support from The National Film Preservation Foundation.)“The terrors and splendors of the human body as the undiscovered, mysterious continent.” –Willard MaasTotal running time: ca. 55 min.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Tenebrae
screenings.description: Argento’s return to his giallo roots after veering off into gonzo horror/fantasy, Tenebrae features Anthony Franciosa as an American author of potboiler thrillers who, promoting a new book in Rome, finds that a murderer is re-enacting his most ghoulish delights of literary fancy. Argento uses the occasion to scale new, dizzying heights of his own, employing bravura crane shots, brazenly baroque lighting, and the iconic moment of a razor slashing through white cotton.

screenings.title: Body Heat
screenings.description: Screenwriter Lawrence Kasdan paid tribute to Double Indemnity with his directorial debut. When the summertime Florida heat enables lawyer William Hurt to scratch an itch with housewife Kathleen Turner, what is there to do about her husband Richard Crenna? Murder, of course! Confidently combining classical storytelling and contemporary sizzle, Body Heat satisfied audiences with a taste for steamy noir stylings and catapulted its two leads into the Hollywood A-list. For Turner in particular (making her feature film debut), Body Heat was the beginning of her reign as one of the queens of 80s cinema.

screenings.title: Devo: Restorations and Revelations
screenings.description: COLLECTED FILM AND VIDEO WORKS 1976-84PRESENTED BY FILM RESTORATIONIST PETER CONHEIMFormed in the wreckage of the Kent State shootings in 1973, where co-founders Gerald V. Casale and Mark Mothersbaugh were students during the massacre, and still blowing the horn five decades later, Akron’s DEVO would take their subversive pop-art to staggering mainstream success. All the while, they considered themselves to be filmmakers as much as they were a “band.”From their first film onward (1976’s THE BEGINNING WAS THE END: THE TRUTH ABOUT DE-EVOLUTION), they fused their love of Dadaist image-making with their constantly shapeshifting music, confounding their record label by plowing their meager promo budgets into companion films for songs. This program unveils painstaking new restorations and reconstructions of much of this pivotal work (including SATISFACTION, FREEDOM OF CHOICE, WHIP IT, and much more) alongside a host of rarely (and never)-seen live footage, encounters with hapless interviewers, and other spud ephemera, curated specially for Anthology Film Archives by film archivist and musician Peter Conheim (Mono Pause, ex-Negativland, Wet Gate, et al).Total running time: ca. 80 min + discussion and Q&A.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!
